Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 49, verse 1:

The surah opens with a most beloved call.

Yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū (49:1): "O you who believe!" This is a call from Allah to those who have faith in Him in the unseen, and by this call Allah stirs enthusiasm and fervour in the hearts of the believers, because the believers' bond with Allah is the bond of faith. The believers have the awareness that they belong to Allah. They have raised the banners of Allah, and on this small planet they are the servants of Allah, the workers of Allah and His army. Allah has sent them here for a purpose, and for this reason He has created love of faith in their hearts and made faith beloved to them, and by enlisting them in this army He has bestowed a favour upon them. Therefore it is best for them to stand at the position where Allah has commanded them to stand, and to stand before Allah as a person stands in a court awaiting a verdict, or as a junior soldier stands before his officer awaiting instructions. He does what he is commanded and prepares for the task he is ordered to undertake, bowing his head completely in submission.

Yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū … inna Allāha samī'un 'alīm (49:1): "O you who believe! Do not put yourselves forward before Allah and His Messenger, and fear Allah. Indeed Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing." O believers, do not present your own proposals before Allah and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), neither concerning your own selves nor concerning the affairs of your surroundings and your life, and do not issue your own decision on any matter before Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ) have decided, and in any matter where Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ) have given a decision, do not issue your own decisions in it.

Qatadah says that some people used to express their desires and proposals, saying how good it would be if rulings came concerning such and such matter; if it happened that way, it would be much better. So Allah disliked these proposals of theirs. 'Awfi says that this verse forbids speaking in the presence of Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ). Mujahid says: do not ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for fatwas needlessly; Allah Himself will send down whatever He wills. Ad-Dahhak says: do not make your own decisions leaving aside Allah, His Messenger (ﷺ), the fundamental principles of the religion and the laws of the Shariah. And 'Ali ibn Talhah reported from Ibn 'Abbas that it means: do not say anything contrary to the Qur'an and the Sunnah.

These are the intellectual and ideological etiquettes in matters concerning Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ). The etiquette of receiving and implementing guidance from Allah is this: obey whatever command comes, and remain silent about the rest. This is the best attitude according to the principles of the religion and the Shariah. It is based on the fear of God and on the reality that Allah sees everything, and all these matters are stated in this brief verse.

Thus was the relationship of the Muslims with Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ). No one would offer his proposal before Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ). No one would express any opinion in the presence of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) unless he asked for it. No one would decide any matter or ruling until he had turned to the words of Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ).

Imam Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah have reported that when the Prophet (ﷺ) was sending Mu'adh ibn Jabal as governor to Yemen, he asked him how he would judge. He replied: "By the Book of Allah." He said: "If you do not find it in the Book of Allah?" He replied: "Then by the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." He said: "If you do not find it in the Sunnah either?" He said: "Then I will make an independent judgment according to my own opinion." Hearing this, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) struck his chest and said: "Praise be to Allah who has granted the envoy of the Messenger of Allah that which pleases the Messenger of Allah."

In another narration, the Prophet (ﷺ) was asking them what day it was and what place they were in. They all knew, but they all answered: "Allah and His Messenger know best," and they said this lest their words should go ahead of Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ).

In the hadith of Abu Bakrah Nufay' ibn al-Harith (may Allah be pleased with him), it comes that on the occasion of the Farewell Pilgrimage the Prophet (ﷺ) asked: "What month is this?" We said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." The Prophet (ﷺ) fell silent, and we thought that perhaps he would give it another name. He said: "Is it not Dhul-Hijjah?" We said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah, it is Dhul-Hijjah." He said: "What city is this?" We said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He fell silent, and we thought that perhaps he would rename it. He said: "Is it not the Sacred City (Balad al-Haram)?" We said: "Yes." He said: "What day is this?" We said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He fell silent, and we thought he might rename it. He said: "Is it not the Day of Sacrifice (Yawm al-Nahr)?" We said: "Yes..."

Such was the state of the respect and reverence of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ): great caution, piety and awe. This respect and reverence arose within them after these verses were revealed, for in these verses it was said: fear Allah, and Allah is All-Hearing and All-Knowing.

The second form of respect and reverence was this: in conversation with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), observe the etiquettes of prophethood. Speak with deference and sincere respect. Let your movements and your voice display reverence. His person, his assembly and his speech should be distinguished. Allah admonishes them in a manner that is most pleasing.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 49, verse 2:

یایھا الذین امنوا ۔۔۔۔۔ وانتم لا تشعرون (49:2) "O you who have believed, do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet, and do not speak loudly to him as you speak to one another, lest your deeds be nullified while you are unaware."

Addressing those who have believed makes clear that your dignity comes from faith, and that faith has been taught to you by Muhammad (ﷺ). Through even a slight carelessness in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), deeds are nullified, and your deeds would become ineffective in the same way that a sturdy animal is destroyed in an instant by poisonous grass. You would have knowledge of it, and yet your deeds would already be lost.

The Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) were so affected by that beloved and dear voice that there is no parallel to it. Imam al-Bukhari narrates from Bishr ibn Safwan, from Nafi' ibn Umar, from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, who says: It nearly happened that two of the Companions of the highest rank, Abu Bakr and Umar, were destroyed. They argued with each other in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ) when the delegation of Banu Tamim came. This was in the ninth year of Hijrah. One said that al-Aqra' ibn Habis should be appointed as the leader; he was from the clients of Ashja'. The other person suggested someone else, whose name I do not remember (in another narration, it is Qa'qa' ibn Ma'bad). Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) said to Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), "You always oppose me." Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said, "I did not intend to oppose you." In this matter their voices were raised. Upon this, this verse was revealed:

یایھا الذین امنوا لاترفعوا ۔۔۔۔۔۔۔ وانتم لا تشعرون (49:2) "O you who have believed, do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet, and do not speak loudly to him as you speak to one another, lest your deeds be nullified while you are unaware."

Ibn al-Zubayr (may Allah be pleased with him) said that after this, Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) would speak so softly to the Prophet (ﷺ) that he would not be heard fully, and the Prophet (ﷺ) would have to ask him again. It is also reported from Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) that when this verse was revealed, he said, "O Messenger of Allah, I will speak to you only in a whisper."

Imam Ahmad narrates from Sulayman ibn al-Mughirah, from Thabit, from Anas ibn Malik, who says that when this verse was revealed:

یایھا الذین امنوا لاترفعوا ۔۔۔۔۔۔۔ وانتم لا تشعرون (49:2) "O you who have believed, do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet, and do not speak loudly to him as you speak to one another, lest your deeds be nullified while you are unaware."

Thabit ibn Qays ibn al-Shammas, who had a very loud voice, said, "I am the one who used to raise my voice above the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). I am among the people of Hellfire, and my deeds have gone to waste." He sat in his house in deep grief. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) noticed that this man was not coming. Some people went to him and said, "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) has noticed your absence. What has happened to you?" He said, "My voice is raised above the voice of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and I used to speak loudly. My deeds have been wasted. Surely I am among the people of Hellfire." These people came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him of what he had said. The Prophet (ﷺ) said, "No, he is among the people of Paradise." Anas (may Allah be pleased with him) said, "He used to walk among us, and we would think, 'There goes a person of Paradise!'"

In short, with the affectionate manner of address, "O you who have believed," the call given to the believers caused them to tremble, and thereafter they sat in the presence of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in great silence and with fear, lest their deeds be nullified without their awareness. Consciously they were very cautious, but their greater fear was that they might suffer loss in a state of unconsciousness, and therefore they were greatly alarmed.

Here Allah has expressed their fear of Allah and their manners in the presence of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in a most remarkable style.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 49, verse 3:

"Indeed, those who lower their voices in the presence of the Messenger of Allah, those are the ones whose hearts Allah has tested for piety. For them is forgiveness and a great reward." (49:3)

Taqwa (God-consciousness, piety) and fear of Allah are a great favour from Allah. It is Allah who chooses hearts for this honour and blessing. After this testing, choice, sincerity and purity of heart, taqwa is then granted to those hearts, so this blessing is given to those hearts which are ready for it and whose worthiness for taqwa becomes evident. Those who lower their voices before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ are chosen for taqwa, and along with this reward, that is, the granting of taqwa, forgiveness is also bestowed upon them.

After the severe warning, this is a deep encouragement. In this way Allah trains the hearts of His free-choosing servants and prepares them for this great task, and with this same method of training, Allah prepared the community of the Companions at the beginning of Islam. These people were upon guidance and possessed light.

It is related from Amir al-Mu'minin Umar ibn al-Khattab (raḍiyallahu ʿanhu) that he heard the voices of two men in the Prophet's Mosque (masjid Nabawi) (ﷺ), and their voices had risen. He came to them and said: "Do you know where you are?" Then he asked them: "Where are you from?" They said: "We are from the people of Ta'if." Upon hearing this, Umar (raḍiyallahu ʿanhu) said: "If you were from the people of Madinah, I would have certainly taught you a lesson."

The scholars of the Ummah understood this matter and said that raising the voice near the blessed grave of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is prohibited, just as during his lifetime raising the voice in the Prophet's Mosque was forbidden. It was prohibited in every condition, out of respect.

After this, reference is made to an event which occurred in 9 AH. After the Conquest of Makkah, delegations were coming from every direction. A delegation of Banu Tamim came to meet the Prophet ﷺ. These people were pure, rough desert dwellers. They stood in front of the Prophet's ﷺ apartments, in which were the Mothers of the Believers, and called out: "Muhammad, come out to us!" The Prophet ﷺ disapproved of their manner, because this manner was extremely crude and disturbing.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 49, verses 4–5:

"Indeed, those who call out to you from behind the chambers, most of them do not understand. And if they had patience until you came out to them, it would have been better for them. And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful." (49:4–5)

Allah said about such people that most of them are not wise. He made their action disliked for them, because it was contrary to Islamic etiquette and contrary to the respect that should have been shown to the person and station of the Prophet (ﷺ). He was the leader and educator of the Muslims and the Prophet of Allah. Therefore they were told that it would have been proper for them to be patient and wait until the Messenger (ﷺ) came out in his usual manner. Allah the Exalted encouraged them to repent, seek forgiveness, and turn back to Allah.

The Muslims understood these etiquettes well. They extended the same treatment not only to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) but to every teacher and every scholar of religion. They did not trouble such personalities inside their homes, and they waited for them to come out. They never attempted to enter the homes of their teachers. It is well known about another famous narrator and scholar, Abu 'Ubayd, that he used to say: "I never knocked on the door of any scholar; I always waited for him to come out."

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 49, verse 6:

"O you who believe, if a sinner comes to you with news, verify it, lest you harm a people in ignorance and then become regretful for what you have done" (49:6).

The first call to the believers was about where they must take their guidance from and where their leadership lies. The second call, with "O you who believe," was about the rights of that leadership and the etiquette of approaching it. These two matters were the foundation of most of the guidance, manners and laws in this surah. For it was also necessary to tell the Muslims where the source of guidance and direction lies, and it was necessary to tell them what the respect and station of the mentor and leader is, so that the leader is respected and the instructions he gives are taken seriously. This third call and guidance is given because in this modern society there must be a policy regarding news, and what should be the reaction of an ordinary person on hearing news? So it was said that this news too should be brought to the leader, and every news item should be investigated and verified.

"O you who believe, if a sinner comes to you with news, verify it, lest you harm a people in ignorance and then become regretful for what you have done" (49:6). Here the sinner is singled out because a sinner may be suspected, and this specification was made so that people do not even doubt the conduct and actions of trustworthy people within the Islamic community, and so that doubt does not become a principle in respect of information instead of trust. For in an Islamic community the principle will certainly be that the reports of its members are relied upon and acted upon. As for the person who is a sinner, his reports must be verified, because he can be suspected. Thus a moderate rule will be established in an Islamic community regarding whether or not to accept and rely upon reports. The news of a sinner is not to be acted upon immediately, lest some injustice befall someone, which would obviously happen through haste, and afterwards the Islamic society would have to feel regret, having done something that displeases Allah, because this would become the source of an action that does not meet the standards of truth and justice.

Ibn Kathir has mentioned that this verse was revealed concerning Walid ibn Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent him to the Banu al-Mustaliq to collect zakat. Ibn Kathir says that Mujahid and Qatadah have stated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent Walid ibn Uqbah to the Banu al-Mustaliq to receive charity from them. They accepted it. He returned and said that the Banu al-Mustaliq were gathering to fight the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and some narrations state that they had also apostatised from Islam. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent Khalid ibn al-Walid (may Allah be pleased with him) and commanded him to investigate the matter and not to be hasty. He went and reached their settlement at night. He sent his spies, and when they returned they reported that these people were firm Muslims; they had given the call to prayer and prayed. In the morning Khalid ibn al-Walid (may Allah be pleased with him) came to them and saw what surprised him. Khalid returned and informed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and then this verse was revealed. Qatadah says that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Verification is from Allah, and haste is from Satan." Likewise other righteous predecessors have also written, such as Ibn Abi Layla, Yazid ibn Ruhan, Dahhak, and Muqatil ibn Hayyan, that this verse was revealed concerning Walid ibn Uqbah. And Allah knows best. (End of quotation from Ibn Kathir)

However, the meaning of the verse is general. The principle is that the statement of a sinner is to be investigated and verified. As for righteous people, their words will be acted upon, because within a believing community the principle is that everyone's word is trusted except that of a sinner. And trust in the word of a righteous person is itself the means of investigation and verification. As for the idea that one should doubt in every matter and regard every report as false unless it is proven, this is not the principle of Islamic society, otherwise no collective work could function in any society. As for righteous people, their words will be acted upon, because within a believing community the principle is that everyone's word is trusted except that of a sinner. And trust in the word of a righteous person is itself the means of investigation and verification. As for the idea that one should doubt in every matter and regard every report as false unless it is proven, this is not the principle of Islamic society, otherwise no collective work could function in any society. Islam allows life to proceed as usual. It certainly adopts precautionary measures, but so that the normal course of life continues, not so that life comes to a standstill. This is the model of the Islamic principle: what its principle is in the receiving and conveying of news.

It is possible that, on the basis of the initial information provided by Walid ibn Uqbah, some people proposed inflicting severe punishment upon the Banu al-Mustaliq. This is because at that time zeal and passion for the religion of Islam were intense, and also because refusing to pay zakat was a great crime. Therefore attention is drawn to this: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is still present among you, so try to understand the presence of the Messenger of Allah, for he has a constant connection with Allah.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 49, verses 7–8:

"And know that among you is the Messenger of Allah" (49:7). This is a matter that every person can understand: that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was present at that time. But if one reflects, it is a great reality. Can anyone imagine that the heavens should be in continuous contact with the earth, that this contact should remain established at all times and be visible to people, and that we should say that the Divine will is turned toward the inhabitants of the earth? People are being told their circumstances. Their secret matters are being told to them. They are being warned about their outward words, and their mistakes are corrected immediately. If someone conceals a thought in his heart, word comes from the heavens that this is what is being thought. Allah tells the Messenger of Allah ﷺ immediately and instructs him to give these instructions to My servants. The truth is that this is a very great matter. It is a very great news and it is a great reality.

Sometimes it may be that, upon finding the Messenger of Allah walking among them, some people do not pay attention to this. Therefore they are being drawn to attention.

"And know that among you is the Messenger of Allah" (49:7). Know this, value it, for it is a great matter.

And know the presence of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Its requirements are that you should not make decisions before a decision comes from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, because the decisions of the Messenger of Allah are based on revelation and inspiration. The decisions that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ makes by the instructions of Allah contain goodness and blessing. And if the Messenger of Allah ﷺ were to follow your own words, you would, through your ignorance, put yourselves into difficulties, because the decisions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ are based on Allah's inspiration. Allah knows best what is good for His servants. The presence of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is indeed a great mercy. The planning of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is the planning of Allah, and the word of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is the word of Allah.

After this, they are drawn to attention that they should value the blessing of faith that has been given to them. It is Allah who made faith beloved to you, made it beautiful in your hearts, you regarded it as precious, your hearts became attached to it, and He made disbelief hateful to your hearts. You came to dislike sinfulness and disobedience. This was a great mercy and generosity of Allah.

"But Allah has endeared to you the faith and has made it beautiful in your hearts, and has made disbelief, wickedness and disobedience hateful to you. Those are the rightly guided. A bounty from Allah and favor. And Allah is Knowing and Wise" (49:7–8).

The opening of the hearts of His servants to faith by Allah, the stirring of their hearts with faith, and the making of faith beautiful for their hearts so that they hasten toward it and can see its perfections and beauties, this is in reality a very great bounty and a very great blessing upon those servants. Compared with it, every blessing is insignificant, even human life and existence itself are insignificant. The existence of a human being and his whole life are of little value and low compared with faith. Soon this verse will come.

"Nay, but Allah confers a favor upon you that He has guided you to faith" (49:17). The detailed discussion will come there, Allah willing.

What is worth reflecting on here is that Allah Almighty is reminding them that it is Allah who intended this good for you, and it is Allah who removed this evil from your hearts, that is, the evil of disbelief, wickedness and disobedience. And it is Allah who, by His grace and generosity, set you on the right path. And He did all this on the basis of His knowledge and wisdom, and assured that as a result there would be goodness and blessing for you. Therefore, do not be hasty, do not put proposals before Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, and do not show zeal before the command, for Allah alone makes the best decisions for you. And as yet the Messenger is among you, so do not take your affairs into your own hands in his presence. This is the purpose of the commentary made on the command that you would create difficulties for yourselves.

Man is very hasty. He does not know what lies ahead of his actions. Man keeps drawing up proposals for his own good and the good of others, but his knowledge is so limited that he does not know what is good and what is evil.

"And man prays for evil as he prays for good, and man is ever hasty" (17:11). If man submits his head before Allah and fully enters into Islam, makes Allah's preference his own preference, and is content that what Allah chooses for him is better than his own choice, that it is more beneficial for him and brings goodness and blessing, then he will feel comfort and tranquility, and his brief life on this earth will pass in great peace and joy. This is a great favor of Allah, and He bestows it upon whom He wills.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 49, verses 9-10:

Surah al-Hujurat 49:9-10: "And if two groups of the believers fight, then make reconciliation between them. But if one of them oppresses the other, then fight against the one that oppresses until it returns to the command of Allah. And if it returns, then make reconciliation between them with justice and act equitably. Indeed, Allah loves those who act justly. The believers are but brothers, so make reconciliation between your brothers and fear Allah that you may receive mercy."

This is a practical law, and it has been established to protect the Islamic society itself from disputes, rivalries, and civil strife. Let it not be that people begin fighting out of personal interests and mere emotions. This law has been revealed in connection with the fact that earlier, because of the news brought by a corrupt person (fasiq), circumstances had arisen that led to war against a group among the believers. The purpose is that investigation should be carried out even before disputes, so that conflict does not begin over false reports, and if it does occur, then this law applies.

In some narrations, the cause of the revelation of this verse is also stated to be a specific incident, or it may be that Allah established this law for such situations without any particular event. In any case, it is an extremely firm law for saving the Islamic society. Through it, the Islamic society and Islamic government remain protected from disorder, sectarianism and civil war, and for the time of collective clash, a path of establishing justice has been prescribed, namely that such matters be resolved through reform and justice. And in this too, the fear of God and the seeking of Allah's mercy have been made the true objective.

Every verse has been revealed on account of a particular incident, or this law has been framed for a hypothetical situation; in any case, although both parties are engaged in fighting, both have been called believers, and despite the possibility that one of them may be the aggressor against the other, it has been said so. Indeed, even despite the possibility that sometimes both may be aggressors.

In such a case, those who are neutral are commanded to reconcile between the two. If, after reconciliation, the aggressive group still does not desist and does not submit to the truth or to a judgment of truth, or if, although the aggression of both has been determined, both refuse to accept the command or reject reconciliation, then it is obligatory upon the Muslims to fight against the rebellious and disobedient group, or against both, and to continue the war against them until both bow in submission before the command of Allah. The command of Allah is that there should be no dispute among the believers under any circumstances. And in the matters over which they differ and on account of which war has broken out, they should bow before the commands of Allah. If the rebels accept the command of Allah, and the believers bring about reconciliation between the two, and this is based upon justice and equity, and the seeking of obedience to Allah and the attainment of His pleasure is the aim, then:

"Indeed, Allah loves those who act justly" (49:9). And after this law, the admonition and observation that all believers are brothers, so there should be brotherhood and connection among the believers. It is this Islamic brotherhood that has gathered you together with one another and, after centuries of wars, has bestowed mutual affection upon you. Therefore, fear Allah. By this you may become worthy of the mercy of God.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 49, verse 10:

﴿Indeed, the believers are but brothers, so make reconciliation between your two brothers; and fear Allah that you may receive mercy.﴾ (49:10) "The believers are indeed brothers, so set right the relations between your brothers, and fear Allah, that mercy may be shown to you." The demand of this brotherhood is that love, peace, cooperation and unity should be the fundamental principle among the Muslim community, and that dispute, discord and fighting should be rare and exceptional. For the establishment of this principle, Muslims have been permitted that, if some believers transgress against others, the rest should fight against the transgressors until they submit to a just decision. This is the fundamental principle of Islamic society. It is a most important measure, and it is decisive in its approach.

The demand of this principle is that when Muslims fight against rebels, they shall not kill any wounded person, and shall not kill any prisoner. And after the battle has been abandoned and weapons have been laid down, no one shall be punished. Nor shall the property of the rebels be taken as spoils of war. This is because the purpose of fighting against the rebel party is to bind them to decisions made on the principles of justice, and to restore the establishment of Islamic brotherhood.

The fundamental principle of the Islamic constitution is that there should be one single imamate or caliphate across all Islamic territories. If allegiance is pledged to one imam, then killing the other is obligatory, and the other imam and his companions should be regarded as rebels. And it is the duty of all Muslims to fight on behalf of the first imam. On this principle, Hadrat Ali (رضي الله عنه) fought against the rebels in the Battle of the Camel and in the Battle of Siffin, and among the Companions, eminent Companions took part with him. Some Companions did not take part in that engagement, such as Sa'd, Muhammad ibn Maslamah, Usamah ibn Zayd and Ibn Umar (رضي الله عنهم). Either it was because the truth was not clear in their minds, that is, their own minds were not clear in this matter as to where the truth lay, so they considered it a fitna; or it was as Imam al-Jassas says, "because they saw that the army with the imam was sufficient and did not need them, so they considered it permissible to sit back." The first possibility appears more correct, and the statements attributed to them also indicate it, as a later narration from Hadrat Ibn Umar (رضي الله عنه) shows that he was deeply remorseful that he had not fought alongside the imam.

Even while this principle stands in its place, this Qur'anic rule can be applied in all kinds of circumstances. For example, in exceptional situations where various imamates are established in different distant regions of the Muslim world. Such situations are exceptional, and under the law of necessity in Islam multiple imamates are considered (permissible), so it is the duty of Muslims to fight alongside each imam against the rebels, if these rebels rebel against an imam, or if one group fights another group within a single government while both groups acknowledge the government. Likewise, it is also the duty of Muslims that if rebels have established their own imamate while multiple imamates exist out of necessity, they should fight alongside the imam against them, and all should unite against that rebel group until it submits to the command of Allah. In this way, this verse gives its judgment in every kind of circumstance.

It is also clear that the system proposed here is a system of arbitration and mediation. Whatever systems humanity has devised, all of them have various defects and errors. The system Islam has prescribed is pure, just and highly principled, because under this system decisions are made according to the law of Allah. In it there is no room for anyone's purpose or personal desire, and it has no flaw or deficiency. Yet wretched humanity still stumbles, falls and walks on wrong paths, although the highway lies open before it.

The Quranic system of life, through which it seeks to establish a virtuous society, has very high standards of etiquette and morals. In it, every individual enjoys dignity of self, and no individual can disgrace another. The dignity of the individual is due to the dignity of society, because the disgrace of one individual is the disgrace of the whole human society. This is because the human community is a single soul, and its honour is one honour. The humiliation of one human being is the humiliation of all humanity.

In this verse, the Quran addresses the Muslims with these sweet words: "O you who believe." Then it forbids one group from mocking another group. Men should not mock other men: it may be that those who are mocked are better than them. Nor should women mock other women: it may be that those who are being mocked are better than those who mock them in the sight of Allah.

This verse indicates that the outward values, goodness and superiorities which some men or some women possess are not in reality true superiorities by which people are weighed in the sight of Allah. Allah has other values, and it may be that these are hidden from those who mock, and only Allah knows them, and by them Allah assigns the weight of those servants. Sometimes the wealthy mock the poor, the strong the weak, a vigorous young man the frail, the intelligent the dull, the one with children the childless, a healthy orphan, a beautiful woman mocks an ugly one, a young woman mocks an old one, a moderate woman mocks one with a disfigured face, a wealthy woman mocks a poor one. But these things belong to this temporary world, for in the scale of Allah these things are completely weightless.

But the Quran does not confine itself only to these directives and indications. Rather, it also arouses the spirit of faithful brotherhood, that those who have believed are one body and one soul, and if one of them taunts another, he is taunting himself.

"And do not defame one another" (49:11). Al-lamz (defamation) means finding fault, but the pronunciation of lamz has a rhythm and a manner. It is not merely fault-finding in meaning, but also indicates physical striking and gesturing with the eyes.

Calling people by names they do not like, and considering being addressed by such names to be mockery, is also forbidden by Islam. It is the right of a believer over a believer that he should not call him by a name he dislikes or considers an insult. Among the etiquettes of the believers is that they should not call one another by such names. The Prophet (ﷺ) changed several names and nicknames of the days of jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance). With his keen sensitivity and his compassionate heart, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) perceived that these people did not like the names whose meanings were bad or from which condemnation arose.

This verse first indicated what the true weight in the scale of Allah is based upon. After that it highlighted the consciousness of Islamic brotherhood, rather it stirred the consciousness of Islamic unity. Then the consciousness of faith was aroused, and believers were warned that the consciousness of faith might be lost from them. By mockery, taunting and calling one another by bad names, you may become transgressors.

"Wretched is the name of wickedness after faith" (49:11). Failing to observe these etiquettes is a kind of apostasy, and it is injustice, and injustice and shirk are one and the same thing.

"And whoever does not repent, they are the wrongdoers" (49:11). These are the etiquettes and morals of the virtuous society of Islam, and its features.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran) on Surah 49, verse 12:

﴿O you who believe! Avoid much suspicion, for indeed some suspicions are sins. And do not spy on one another, and let none of you backbite another. Would any of you like to eat the flesh of his dead brother? You would detest it. So fear Allah. Indeed Allah is Most Relenting, Most Merciful.﴾ (49:12)

This verse is another protective barrier around the virtuous society, one in which the freedom and honour of the individual are preserved. In the same way, people are taught how to express their consciousness and their conscience, and what their thinking about others will be in the future. This is expressed in a most effective manner.

It begins with that beloved call: "O you who believe!" Then it says: refrain from excessive and evil suspicion of others. Do not base your judgements about anyone on doubts and misgivings. And the reason for this is stated:

﴿For indeed some suspicions are sins.﴾ (49:12) The emphasis is on "some suspicion", meaning that some suspicions are sins, that is, evil suspicion is a sin. Since no one can know which of his suspicions is correct and which is wrong, no evil suspicion should be held about anyone.

Therefore, Muslims should hold good opinions of one another and keep their hearts clear of every kind of doubt and misgiving. In a society where there are no doubts and suspicions against one another, people's hearts are pure towards one another. No one suspects another; every person is content with the other. The extent of the happiness of life in such a society cannot even be imagined.

But in the luminous society of Islam, this principle is not only current in individual dealings; it is also an important principle in collective affairs, and through it the rights of people are protected. In the pure society of Islam, no one is seized merely on the basis of doubt and suspicion, nor are cases founded on mere suspicions. People are not thrown into prisons on the basis of doubt. Rather, bringing someone within the circle of investigation on the basis of suspicion is itself a crime. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If you begin to entertain suspicion, then there is no (further) investigation." (Tabarani) That is, if anyone does investigate, he should begin by regarding people as innocent, so that their freedom is restored, their rights are protected, and their trust and dignity are re-established. A person should be seized only when it is well known that he has committed a crime. No one may be harassed merely for investigation or on the basis of suspicion.

Glory be to Allah, how lofty is the station to which this verse raises human freedoms, human rights, human trust and confidence, and human dignity! Today's so-called civilised and democratic societies cannot reach this level, the level to which Islam practically raised the conscience of a society, and then established this standard in practice in a society fourteen hundred years ago. Advancing this very principle further, the sphere of suspicion is further restricted.

﴿And do not spy.﴾ (49:12) Often spying (tajassus, probing into others' private affairs) arises from suspicion, and sometimes it is done to discover people's secrets and to learn their weaknesses. The Qur'an treats this base act from the moral point of view, and purifies the hearts of people from such evil thoughts, so that no one seeks out another's hidden circumstances or pursues his weaknesses. For in moral purification, the aim is precisely that the hidden weaknesses of people should not be exposed.

But this principle goes beyond a mere moral code. It also concerns collective purity and legal and administrative affairs. In Islam, certain freedoms, certain honours and certain dignities of people are such that no violation of them is permissible in any circumstances.

In the virtuous society of Islam, people's lives, their homes, their secrets and their hidden weaknesses are protected. For no reason may anyone lay a hand on another's life, another's home, another's secrets or another's weaknesses. Even the institutions of investigation and inquiry into crimes are not permitted to spy in Islam. Islam deals with people according to their outward conditions, and it is not lawful for anyone to enter another's house and find out his inner state. Islam seizes only upon outward crimes and violations. No one is seized on the basis of suspicion or expectation that these people have committed a crime or are about to commit one. In Islam, arrest follows the commission of a crime. Other safeguards for arrest exist as well, which are specific to each crime.

Imam Abu Dawud narrated through Abu Bakr ibn Shaybah, from Abu Mu'awiyah, from A'mash, from Zayd ibn Wahb, who said: Ibn Mas'ud came, and it was said to him: "This is so-and-so, and wine is dripping from his beard." He said: "We have been forbidden from spying. But if something becomes apparent to us, that it has been committed, then we seize (him)." Mujahid said: "Do not spy; seize people for their outward actions. What Allah has concealed, leave concealed."

Imam Ahmad narrated from Dujayn the scribe, from Uqbah, who said: I said to Uqbah: "Some of our neighbours drink wine. I am going to call the police against them, so that they may seize them." Uqbah said: "Do not do that, but advise them and threaten them." He said: they did so, but they did not desist. Then Dujayn came back to him and said: "I have stopped them, but they did not stop. Now I am going to call the police for them." Uqbah said: "You will be destroyed! Do not do so. I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Whoever conceals a believer's fault, it is as if he has brought back to life a girl buried alive.'" (Abu Dawud Sijistani)

Sufyan al-Thawri narrated from Rashid ibn Sa'd, from Mu'awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan, who said: I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: "If you pursue the hidden matters of people, you will ruin them, or you will nearly ruin them." Upon this, Abu al-Darda said: "This is a saying which Mu'awiyah (may Allah be pleased with him) heard from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ); may Allah benefit him through it." (Abu Dawud)

In this way, this verse of the Qur'an became a constitutional article of Islam's political system, and it did not remain merely a sermon consisting of moral and spiritual reform. It became a protection for people's fundamental rights and personal freedoms, and in Islamic law and constitution their rights were so safeguarded that, from far and near and under no pretext, it became impossible to lay hands on them.

Where are these far-reaching rights? Where is this lofty horizon? And where are those rights of which today's Western democratic governments boast? Where are they? And that too after fourteen hundred years! After this, in a remarkable style of speech and in a most humane and moral manner, the Qur'an prohibits backbiting (ghiba) and slander.

﴿And let none of you backbite another. Would any of you like to eat the flesh of his dead brother? You would detest it.﴾ (49:12) Do not backbite one another. Then a scene is presented which affects even the most hard-hearted person: one brother is eating the flesh of his dead brother. Having shown this scene, it is said: if you have disliked this scene, then you have disliked backbiting too.

A comprehensive comment on the things prohibited in this verse: that is, evil suspicion, spying and backbiting, and that you should fear Allah. And there is an indication that if anyone has committed a fault, he should seek forgiveness and ask for pardon.

﴿And fear Allah. Indeed Allah is Most Relenting, Most Merciful.﴾ (49:12) This verse runs through the life of the community of Muslims like blood. It becomes the guardian of all fundamental rights in that society, a way of thinking for human ideas and perceptions, and a standard of conduct for Islamic morality. And in the very manner of the Qur'an, the Messenger (ﷺ) warns people against even the conception and imagining of evil suspicion, spying and backbiting.

Imam Abu Dawud narrated from Qa'bi, from Abd al-Aziz ibn Muhammad, from Abd, from his father, and from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked: "O Messenger of Allah, what is backbiting?" He said: "That you mention your brother in a way that he would dislike." It was said: "If I say something that is actually in him?" He said: "If what you say is in him, then you have backbitten him; and if it is not in him, then you have slandered him." (Tirmidhi, Ahmad)

Imam Abu Dawud narrated from Musaddad, from Yahya, from Sufyan, from Ali ibn Aqmar, from Abu Hudhayfah, and from Aishah (may Allah be pleased with her), who said: I said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Such-and-such things about Safiyyah are enough for you," (Musaddad said: she meant her shortcomings). Upon this, the Messenger (ﷺ) said: "You have said a word which, if it were mixed into the sea, would change its colour." Aishah said: "And I once mentioned a certain person before him, and he said: 'I do not like to relate about a person, even if I were given such-and-such.'"

Imam Abu Dawud narrated from Anas ibn Malik that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When I was taken on the journey of the Ascension (mi'raj), I passed by some people whose nails were of copper, with which they were scratching their faces and chests. I said: 'Who are these people, O Jibril (peace be upon him)?' He said: 'These are the people who eat people's flesh and dishonour them.'"

When Ma'iz and the woman of Ghamid confessed to adultery, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered that both be stoned, because they had confessed, and then insisted on their confession and said: "Purify us," the Prophet (ﷺ) heard one man say to another: "Did you not see this man, whose sin Allah concealed, but whose soul did not leave him alone until he was killed with stones like a dog?" After this, the Messenger (ﷺ) went on. On the way there was the carcass of a donkey, and he said: "Where are so-and-so and so-and-so?" He said to those two: "Get down, and eat from this carrion." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, may Allah forgive you! Is carrion of a donkey eaten?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "What you have eaten of your brother's flesh is now more difficult than this. By Him in whose hand is my soul, he is now plunging into the rivers of Paradise." (Ibn Kathir)

Through this kind of continuous training, Islamic society was purified and, being purified, it reached a lofty station. This was a human dream which became a reality in Islamic history itself.

* * *

Having called the believers again and again with this sweet voice, "O you who believe!", and having raised them to the luminous horizon of humanity, to the lofty heights of the psychological etiquette of man, of collective etiquette, of fundamental human rights, and of the guarantees and assurances of human dignity, honour and freedom, and having made their sensitivity extremely keen and equipped them with the weapons of God-fearing and awe of Allah, the address now turns to the whole of humanity. O all humankind, of various colours, various races, various ages and various regions: your origin is one, your fundamental values are one. And through these very values, this community of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) attained those heights.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 49, verse 13:

"O mankind, indeed We have created you from male and female and made you peoples and tribes that you may know one another. Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you. Indeed, Allah is Knowing and Acquainted." (49:13)

O people of various nations and various colours! O people of different peoples and tribes! Your origin is one. So do not quarrel among yourselves, do not fight with one another, and do not walk on separate paths. O people, the One who is calling you is the same One who created you. He created you from a male and a female. Does He tell you why He has divided you into nations and tribes? It is not so that you may cut each other's throats and wage wars. It is only for introduction and connection. As for the difference of language and colour, the difference of temperament and disposition, and the difference of ability and capacity, these are differences and variety because of which strife and war are unjustified. Rather, these things should become a cause of cooperation in discharging mutual responsibilities. Moreover, through these differences all the needs of society are fulfilled. In the scales of Allah, colour, race, language and homeland have no value at all. In Islam, all values are brought into a single balance, and according to it the principles of good and evil are determined. That is:

"Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you." (49:13) "Among you, the one who is noble is the one who is most righteous among you." And in truth, the one who is honoured is indeed the one who is honoured in the sight of Allah. Allah weighs you by His knowledge and awareness.

"Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you." (49:13) "Among you, the most noble is the one who is most righteous among you." And in truth, the one who is honoured is indeed the one who is honoured in the sight of Allah. Allah weighs you by His knowledge and awareness.

"Indeed, Allah is Knowing and Acquainted." (49:13) "Indeed Allah is All-Knowing and All-Aware."

Thus all distinctions are abolished, and all false values are abolished. One single measure remains with one single value: the scale of humanity and the value of God-fearing, and everything else is worthless.

Thus on this earth all these disputes and quarrels disappear, and all those base aims and objectives are abolished for which people pounce upon one another as dogs pounce upon a bone. In this way the causes of affection and love arise among people. Allah becomes the Deity of all. All are created from one origin, and one human banner remains, under which all people stand, namely Allah... In Islam, this banner, the single human banner, was raised fourteen hundred years ago so that humanity could be freed from the satanic banners of colour, race, nation and homeland. Freedom is to be granted from the fanaticism of colour, the fanaticism of race, the fanaticism of land, the fanaticism of tribe and the fanaticism of family. All these fanaticisms have emerged from jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance before Islam) and are for the promotion of jahiliyyah. They come in various colours and garments, and they come under various names, but all of them are kinds of naked jahiliyyah. There is no Islamic garment for them.

Islam waged jihad against all kinds of jahiliyyah fanaticism so that it might establish its universal human system under the banner of the Lord of the worlds, not under the banner of race or tribe. These are all counterfeit banners, and Islam does not recognise them.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "You are all the children of Adam, and Adam was created from clay. Let those who boast of their forefathers give up that practice, or else it is very easy for Allah to make them lower than a dung beetle." (Al-Bazzar). And concerning jahiliyyah fanaticism, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Leave it, for it is foul." (Muslim)

This is the principle upon which the Islamic system is founded, which is a universal human system and which builds a universal human society. Islam established this society and system fourteen hundred years ago, while humanity still attempts to imitate it, because humanity has not yet begun to walk upon the straight path of Islam towards that society, that is, standing under the banner of Allah, Lord of the worlds. This is the one banner, the banner of the doctrine of tawhid, under which the whole of humanity can stand.

Now at the end of this surah, the reality of faith and its importance are explained, and this is stated in refutation of the Bedouins who claimed to have faith. These people would impose their favour upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, saying that they had become Muslims, and they did not reflect on the favour Allah had shown to people by sending the call to faith.

These verses were revealed concerning the rural Muslims of the tribe of Banu Asad. They said that they "believed" (ﺁﻣﻨﺎ). They said this at the time they were entering Islam. They also said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "O Messenger of Allah ﷺ, we have accepted Islam, but we never fought with you, whereas other Arabs fought battles against you." So Allah informed them that the notion lodged in their minds, that they had accepted Islam, was mistaken. They had submitted to the Islamic state, but their hearts had not yet reached the rank of faith. From this it is known that the reality of faith had not yet settled in their hearts, and their souls had not yet drunk the cup of faith.

﴿Qul lam tu'minu wa lakin qulu aslamna wa lamma yadkhuli al-iman fi qulubikum﴾ (49:14): "Say to them: You have not believed, but rather say, 'We have submitted,' for faith has not yet entered your hearts."

Nevertheless, Allah said that they would be fully rewarded for their deeds, and no part of their deeds would be lost. Since this Islam had not yet entered their hearts and reached their inner selves so that it became firm and reassuring faith, it is sufficient that they be given the reward of good for these good deeds, and that these deeds not be lost like the deeds of the disbelievers. And with Allah, the reward of such Muslims will not be diminished, so long as they remain obedient and submissive.

﴿Wa in tuti'u Allaha wa rasulahu la yalitkum min a'malikum shay'an﴾ (49:14): "If you obey Allah and His Messenger, He will not reduce anything from the reward of your deeds." Because Allah is extremely merciful and generous. He accepts from His servants even the first step in the path of Islam and faith; He is pleased with them through obedience and submission alone, and after that faith and tranquillity come into the heart on their own.

﴿Inna Allaha Ghafurun Rahim﴾ (49:14): "Indeed Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful." After this, the true faith was described.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 49, verse 15:

إنما المؤمنون الذين ... هم الصادقون (49:15) "The believers are only those who have believed in Allah and His Messenger, then did not doubt, and strove with their wealth and their lives in the cause of Allah. It is they who are the truthful."

The reality of faith is that one's conviction in Allah and His Messenger reaches the heart. It is a conviction in which no doubt or unease remains in the heart. It is a conviction that is firm, in which there is no wavering or restlessness, and no misgiving or doubt. There should be no instability in the heart or the consciousness, and from it should arise the deeds of jihad with the self and jihad with wealth. When the heart tastes the sweetness of faith and becomes content and steadfast upon it, its effect manifests in deeds and bodily actions. It becomes visible in the practical world. The believer strives that the faith which dwells in his feeling, his consciousness, and his inner self should also become apparent in the affairs of the environment around him. The inner picture of faith in a person's heart and its practical form in the believer's surroundings cannot be separated from one another. If such a separation existed, the believer would constantly suffer distress. Therefore he comes forward to strive with his wealth and his self. This is the manifestation and the surge of the believer's personal faith, which takes practical shape, because the believer wishes to bring the picture of his religion into action, so that this picture truly becomes a picture. Thus the believer's struggle with his environment is a purely personal matter for a believer... A believer cannot bear a two-fold life, where his religion is one thing and his environment another. Nor is it possible for him to remove faith from his heart and go along with whichever way the wind blows. Therefore, the moment a person becomes a believer, his struggle with his environment begins, which is called jihad. And this jihad continues until the jahiliyyah that surrounds the believer is eliminated.

Ulaika hum as-sadiqun (49:15): "It is such people who are truthful." They are truthful in their creed and their outlook. If they say that we are believers, but the faith in their hearts does not, armed, clash with the environment around them that is contrary to faith in the practical form of life, then understand that there is no faith. Such a person is not truthful in creed and convictions.

In this verse, the restrictive particle "innama" (only) is noteworthy.

Innama al-mu'minuna alladhina amanu billahi wa rasulihi thumma lam yartabu (49:15): "The believers are truly only those who believed in Allah and His Messenger, then did not doubt." In short, faith is not merely worship. Faith is not merely the name of a mental state, nor is it any alteration in the state that exists within the self. After faith, "then did not doubt" (lam yartabu). This restriction in this verse is similar to the following verse:

Inna alladhina qalu rabbuna Allahu thumma istaqamu: "Those who said, 'Our Lord is Allah,' and then remained steadfast." Saying that Allah is our Lord, not doubting, and adopting steadfastness indicates that at times doubts and disturbances arise in the self of a believer as a result of various experiences, various difficulties, and some severe trials. In the ups and downs of life, people sometimes face severe hardships, but in the heart of a true believer no unease and no doubt arises. He remains firm, and no instability arises within him. He has complete trust in his Lord, and he advances on the straight path with full steadfastness, and he keeps on advancing.

The purpose of expressing it in this manner is to alert the people of faith that on this path there are many difficulties, places of slipping, and places of danger, so that a believer may strengthen his resolve, prepare himself well, and walk straight ahead. And when mist spreads over the horizon, he should not begin to doubt, and should not become a prey to storms and tempests.

Following this same theme, they are told that Allah knows even the hearts and intentions of people. It is Allah who informs you of the matters of your hearts, and Allah does not learn from you.

Say, [O Prophet]: ﴿Do you inform Allah about your religion, while Allah knows whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and Allah is Knowing of everything?﴾ (49:16). Man makes sweeping claims about his knowledge, though he knows nothing of his own self. He does not have full information even about the conscious world of his own self. Nor does he know the complete reality of his own soul, nor of the conscious and the subconscious. Man also does not know how his intellect functions, because when a person is performing an action, he cannot himself observe (observation) his own brain. And when he thinks about his own self, the action he is performing stops, so there remains nothing to observe. And when a person is engaged in some task, he cannot monitor it. Therefore, man is incapable of true recognition of his own self, and incapable of discovering how the human brain works. Yet this is precisely the thing in which man takes pride.

﴿And Allah knows whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ (49:16). True knowledge belongs to Allah; we only know the apparent. Allah is aware of the essence and reality of everything. The knowledge of Allah is comprehensive, all-encompassing, unlimited, eternal and everlasting.

﴿And Allah is Knowing of everything﴾ (49:16). That is, everything to which the term "thing" applies. He has encompassing knowledge of it. Having stated that you have not reached the reality of faith and have not grasped its true nature, the address turns toward the Holy Prophet ﷺ: these people place their Islam as a favour upon you. Their boasting of their favour is itself evidence that they have not been able to grasp the reality of faith, and that they have not yet tasted the sweetness of faith.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (*Fi Zilal al-Quran*, Urdu translation) on Surah 49, verse 17 (part 1 of 2):

﴿They consider it a favour to you that they have accepted Islam. Say: Do not consider your Islam a favour to me; rather, Allah has conferred a favour upon you that He guided you to faith, if you are truthful.﴾ (49:17)

They claimed as a favour that they had embraced Islam, and their assumption was that they were believers. The reply came: do not boast of your Islam. If you are truthful in your claim to Islam and faith, then the favour is from Allah.

The fact that Allah revealed this verse in refutation of them reveals a great truth, one of which even great people are heedless. We should reflect on it a little. Some of the people of faith also become heedless of it.

Allah has bestowed great favours upon the inhabitants of the earth, and among them faith is the greatest. The greatest favour is the very existence of the human being and ... can be understood. Likewise, the necessities, prerequisites and needs of human life can be understood, such as health, provisions and life itself. But faith is the greatest of all these blessings.

This is the favour that makes a person's whole life purposeful, meaningful and distinguished, and because of faith a person's role on this earth becomes very real and distinguished.

Because of faith, the first change that occurs in a person, provided the reality of faith settles in the mind, is that the believer's conception of the universe becomes very broad. Because of this conception, a person becomes connected with this universe, a role for the person in it is determined, and the value of everything in his environment, whether persons, events or things, is determined in his eyes. He traverses this brief journey on this planet Earth with complete tranquillity and reaches Allah. He becomes disillusioned with the universe spread around him and becomes familiar with his Creator, who is the Creator of him and of this universe. He becomes aware of his own importance and greatness, and that he can discharge his roles in such a way that Allah is pleased with him, and that he can become a source of goodness and blessing for the creatures of this universe and for human beings.

In another respect, expansion also comes into a person's conception: he goes beyond the limits of time and space. He also comes out of the limits of his small self and enters the expanses of this universe, in which Allah has placed boundless powers and countless secrets hidden. A person advances so far that he too becomes, in a sense, limitless.

Since a human being, in respect of his species, is one individual of humanity, and returns to one origin, therefore at the beginning man received his humanity from the spirit of Allah. This He bestowed by breathing His spirit into a clay framework, and through this breathing of the spirit this human being is joined with the light of the higher realm. This light is not confined within the limits of heaven and earth. It is beyond them, with neither beginning nor end, and it is not confined within the limits of place and time. This light and spirit is what makes a human being human. When this fact settles within the soul of a person, then first of all a person rises high in his own eyes. This conception makes a person honoured within his own feelings and gives him the awareness of extreme light and universality. His feet walk on the earth, but his spirit flutters to join its source, from which it was given spirit and light at the beginning and which gave it this wondrous colour of life.

And this person, in respect of his nation and community, is an individual of the Muslim ummah. This is the one and only ummah which, through the ups and downs of history, has for ages moved forward as an honourable caravan. Its leadership has been in the hands of Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus and Muhammad (peace be upon them). It is sufficient for a human being that this fact settles in his heart: that he is a branch of that blessed tree whose roots have spread far into the depths of history and whose branches have extended far into the heavens. This conception alone is sufficient to grant a person a lofty taste for life. Whoever attains it adopts new sensations of life, and within his life another life is born, and this life he receives from this ideological lineage.

No, human conception has not yet stopped. It goes beyond his own self, his own ummah and his own humanity, and by means of his spirit it gathers within itself this entire universe as well, for it is that Being who created it, the One who created the human being and who bestowed upon him a spirit, and because of whom he has become the bridegroom of the universe. Then his faith tells him that this universe also possesses a living existence. It is created from living atoms. Everything in it has a spirit. This whole universe also has a spirit. The spirits of human beings and the great spirit of this universe are in truth both turned towards the Creator, the Exalted. All of them call upon Allah, glorify Him, are engaged in His praise and obedience, and have completely submitted to the commands of Allah. Thus the human being becomes a part of the whole of this great universe. He is neither separate from it nor apart from it. He proceeds from Allah and, through his spirit, is turned towards Him, and in the Hereafter he too will return to Him. Therefore this human being is greater than his limited self. He is as great as the greatness of the universe that he can fix in his mind. He is familiar with all the spirits of his environment, and then he is familiar with the spirit that Allah breathed into him. At this point he reflects that he can unite with this entire universe, however vast and wide it may be, and that it is possible for him to perform outstanding deeds in it, to be the cause of great events, to influence everything and to be influenced by it. Then it is possible for him to benefit from that power which created him and created the universe spread throughout his environment: that great power which is neither weakened, nor diminished, nor absent. That is, Allah, the Great, the Most High.

Within this measure of broad conception, this human being then weighs all things, all events, all persons, all values, all arrangements, all purposes and all stations with a completely new measure. He comes to know what his true role in this universe is, and what his purpose of existence in this universe is. He is one of the values of Allah in this universe. Therefore Allah may turn him in whatever direction He wills and use him in whatever manner He wishes. Thus he then traverses this journey of life on this planet with steadfastness, with clear insight and with a familiar conscience.

When a person, from this viewpoint, grasps the reality of this universe that is present in his environment, then he determines what his role in this world is, and what powers have been given to him here to discharge that role. Through this knowledge and recognition he attains contentment, peace and joy: that regarding whatever is happening in his environment and whatever it presents to him, he knows who its mover is, or from where it itself is coming, and why it has come, where it is going, and what it will find there. For he knows what his purpose of life is, and whatever befalls him is his destiny, and must come to pass. And this world is the field of the Hereafter, and for small and great deeds he will be rewarded. He was not created in vain. Nor is he an unbridled camel, nor will he go alone.

Through this conception and awareness, human life is freed from the anxiety of restlessness, perplexity, bewilderment and the worry of ignorance concerning its beginning and its end. He is neither restless about the path nor distressed about his coming and going. Listen to Omar Khayyam, who is distressed: "The garment of life was put upon me without my being asked. During this life I kept thinking various thoughts. Soon the garment of life will be taken off me, and I do not know why I came and where I am to go."

Therefore a believer holds with complete inner tranquillity and with great gladness of heart, and with a cheerful and radiant face says that the garment of life has been put on him by the hand of divine power. That divine power acts in this universe as the All-Knowing, the All-Powerful. And the hand that has clothed him with the garment of life is firmer, merciful and generous. Therefore there was no need for any consultation with him, because a human being cannot conceive what the All-Knowing, the All-Powerful can conceive. And the All-Knowing, the All-Powerful has clothed a human being with the garment of life for this purpose: that he has a role to play in this universe. He will be affected by the things within this universe and will affect them, and the role that he has to play is in harmony with the role that all things in this world are performing, whether living or non-living, from beginning to end.

Thus a believer knows why he has come, and he also knows where he has to go. He does not fall into any intellectual confusion. Rather, he performs this journey and this role of his with complete tranquillity, with perfect certainty and with full assurance. Sometimes this believer advances so far in the degree of faith that he performs this role with such joy and delight that he is aware of the beauty of this gift of life, and considers it a great bounty, and regards this span of life and its garment as a royal robe of honour. That King who is subtle, all-aware, beautiful, loving and merciful, and the role that is to be performed here, however much it may become a cause of hardship, he can perform it and reach the Lord of Majesty and Honour.

And such disturbing awareness disappears solely because of faith. I myself was caught for a long time in this kind of awareness, in most painful distresses, during the period when I had not yet been granted the good fortune to come under the protective shade of the Qur'an, and at the time when Allah had not yet taken my hand and admitted me into His protective shelter. This awareness was present in my soul, and in accordance with "the sorrowful heart makes sorrowful..." I had wrapped this awareness around the whole universe.

The universe stood bewildered: whither is it going, why is it going, and how is it going?
If it were to go, then it would be a vain struggle, a transient world, a futile effort and a dejected end; and when the drum of death sounds, whether it wishes or not, it must go.

Today I know, and by the grace and mercy of Allah I know, that no struggle is wasted. This is the recompense and punishment of one's deeds. No effort goes in vain. The outcome conforms to one's wish, and the destination is the Just Allah and the Compassionate, Merciful Lord. And this universe will not remain stationary here. The spirit of this universe is turned towards the Lord, the Exalted, and is glorifying and praising Him, and it is moving according to His will, and according to that law which He has prepared for it, in complete submission and contentment, going with obedience to His command.

I think that in the world of thought and consciousness, this is also a very great wealth for a human being, and apart from this there are benefits in terms of the body and nerves as well, and in beauty of performance, struggle, influence and impression.

Faith is, just as it is a material force for the human body and spirit, also an impelling force. As soon as faith takes root in a heart, it comes out of the body again in the form of practical struggle. The form of faith that is in the mind keeps pace with the form of faith that exists outwardly in the practical world, and faith takes possession of the motive faculties of a person and drives him onto the path.

"This is the secret for which the power of belief is latent within the self, and likewise the secret of the increase of psychological powers because of being a believer is also this. The wonders and miracles that have proceeded, and continue to proceed, into the world because of an ideology, their secret is this. Because of these miracles the face of life changes day after day. It is faith and ideology alone for which people sacrifice even this transient life, and step into that life which is never transient. Even a very weak and small person walks with his head held high before a king or a dictator, and pays no heed to the powers of fire and iron. Then the time comes when gunpowder is defeated before faith. It is not merely one person who defeats these great powers, but an ideology which reduces these powers to dust. Indeed it is the source of that great power of faith from which the human soul draws strength. This source never dries up, never diminishes, and never grows weak."

This is the translation. Note that the passage contains a Qur'anic quotation which I render in English within ﴿ ﴾.

These remarkable transformations which an ideology, an individual and a society undergo cannot be brought about by a doctrine founded upon myths and fables, one that is incomprehensible, or merely based on fear, astonishment and imagination. Rather, it is a belief that can be comprehended and is built upon firm principles. True religious belief is that which unites a person with the outward and inward forces of this universe, and which instills confidence and tranquility within the soul of man. It also creates within him a strength with which he confronts all those transient and perishable false powers, and he is certain that in the end he will be victorious. This confidence is obtained from the Being of Allah. And this belief is such that it tells a person that he is connected with the events of his environment, and with all the things and all the people around him. This belief shows him his destination and tells him his end. It gathers all his powers and sets them in one direction. This is the secret of the power of belief: it gathers all forces and turns them around a single axis. It gives them one direction. People come to know their goal, and they advance towards their objective with great strength, certainty and confidence.

In short, the power of beliefs and ideologies increases in this way too: they move in the same direction in which this entire universe moves. All the cosmic forces, whether outward or inward, move along with them, because all the forces within the universe are travelling on the path of faith. Thus, for a believer, these cosmic forces become companions on the journey, and in this way the power of faith and the cosmic forces together attack falsehood, even though falsehood may appear to be a great power outwardly and dazzling to the eyes; yet through the power of faith it will be shattered to pieces.

Allah said to us: ﴿They consider it a favour to you that they have embraced Islam. Say: "Do not consider your Islam a favour to me; rather, Allah has conferred a favour upon you that He has guided you to faith, if you are truthful."﴾ This is that great bounty whose owner is also Allah, and whose giver is also Allah. And Allah entrusts the wealth of faith to the one whom He knows to be deserving of this great grace.

Allah spoke the truth. Whoever befriends these truths and knowledge, and attains these meanings and this awareness, and within them he comes alive, and he lives within this small planet a brief life under ordinary circumstances, has in fact lost nothing at all. And whoever is deprived of this wealth, even if he lives a life of luxury and comfort, eating and drinking excessively the way cattle eat and drink plenty, let him know that these cattle are better than him, for they, by their nature, are obedient to their Generous Creator.

Allah knows the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and Allah sees what you do. (49:18)

Allah knows the hidden things of the heavens and the earth. He knows what is in hearts and knows the human consciousness. He sees what people actually do. He knows not only the words that come from people's tongues, but also the conscious feelings that surge in their hearts, and the deeds that result from those inner feelings.

This great surah, consisting of eleven verses, lays down for the believers extremely important guidelines and most exalted and pure guidelines, and points to great principles and realities in the depths of human consciousness and conscience.
